title: Ch. 2 — Stalking with Stories
paragraphs: This chapter is Basso's argument with a stereotype — that Apaches are mystically inclined and correspondingly inarticulate — and his teacher is Nick Thompson: elderly, partially paralyzed, a medicine man and singer, incorrigible and very funny, whom Basso nicknames Slim Coyote. Nick's instruction is one imperative: learn the names of all these places. Whitemen need paper maps, he observes. We have maps in our minds.

Four short statements set the terms. Annie Peaches, aged seventy-seven: the land is always stalking people; the land makes people live right; the land looks after us. Ronnie Lupe: our children are losing the land, it no longer goes to work on them, they do not know the stories about what happened at these places, and that is why some get into trouble. Nick Thompson: we live with money now, but the land still looks after us, because we know the names of the places where everything happened, so we stay away from badness. And Benson Lewis, who says he thinks of a mountain as if it were his maternal grandmother: its name is like a picture, and stories go to work on you like arrows.

To show why arrows, Basso first lays out the shape of Apache speech. It divides into ordinary talk, prayer, and narrative; narrative divides again by when it happened and what it is for. Myths, to tell of holiness, are long and belong to the time of creation and to medicine men. Historical tales — 'ágodzaahí, to tell of that which has happened — are short, set in the time when the Apache were developing themselves, and begin and end with a place-name. Sagas, to tell of pleasantness, are modern and for entertainment. Gossip covers the present. Only the historical tale is a weapon, and its purpose is to criticize social delinquents.

The hunting metaphor is the chapter's centre. Someone hunts you — a grandmother, a grandfather, an uncle, anyone — and tells a story about what happened long ago; other people may be present, but you know it is aimed at you. A weak arrow bounces off. A strong one goes in deep and starts working on your mind: you feel weak, you do not want to eat or talk, you think only of what you did wrong. That story is changing you, making you want to replace yourself. Later you may try to pull the arrow out, but you cannot, because you will keep seeing the place — and if you cannot see it you will hear its name and see it in your mind. It will keep stalking you even if you go across oceans, and it will keep stalking you after the person who shot you has died.

Nick's model tale is set at Men Stand Above Here And There, where an Apache policeman released the prisoner he had arrested — a man who had killed a cow off the reservation. The policeman had sided with outsiders against one of his own, and when he died his relatives dispensed with the customary mortuary ritual, disowning him completely. Aimed at a young man who parades whitemen's attitudes and mannerisms, the tale needs no commentary; the response Basso records is simply, I know that place. It stalks me every day. The negative proof arrives from Wilson Lavender, who trained as a mechanic in Los Angeles and describes losing the names and losing the ability to live right as a single process.

The chapter closes with a disciplinary complaint. Human ecologists, having committed themselves to statistical regularities and functional interdependencies, are obliged to treat the meanings of environments as epiphenomena outside their proper concern — and so they have become largely uninterested in what people take their environments to mean. Basso's reply is that ecological models are pitched at a systemic level well removed from the individual, and it is individuals, not institutions, who make and act on cultural meanings. He wants a cultural ecology that is cultural in the fullest sense. Societies must survive, he writes, but social life is more than just surviving, and cultural meanings are epiphenomenal only for those who choose to make them so.
